items.title: Many drugs work by binding to a specific target in the body and blocking or changing what it does. An important first st
items.content:
Many drugs work by binding to a specific target in the body and blocking or changing what it does. An important first step in the drug development process is designing a molecule that can bind tightly to its target. Traditionally, that's meant weeks or months of expert work per target, sifting through a large number of candidates to identify the few that work.

We wanted to test if Claude could successfully design novel protein binders from scratch (also called de novo design). With a protein design prompt written by a human expert, Claude autonomously designed protein binders against 14 out of 15 targets.

We then worked with Adaptyv Bio and Twist Bioscience, who independently built and tested the proteins Claude designed.

items.title: 1/2 Thanks Gavin for an especially thoughtful exchange. I don't usually spend much time on social media but I wanted to
items.content:
1/2 Thanks Gavin for an especially thoughtful exchange. I don't usually spend much time on social media but I wanted to engage here because it really brings out the heart of an important conversation.

First, on regulation, I think that “either concentrate it in the hands of a chosen few companies and politicians via regulation or distribute it widely” is a false choice.  I know that there’s a sort of Silicon Valley shorthand where regulation = regulatory capture = concentration of power, but I’ve always found this to be an overly simplified picture of the world.  Many people outside this bubble think of regulation as something that constrains corporate power and benefits ordinary people.  I don’t necessarily agree with that perspective either, rather I think it’s complicated and really depends on what the “regulation” consists of.  But in particular I think that those in the “regulation = regulatory capture = concentration of power” frame often underrate the decentralizing power of objective and fair institutional processes.  A crude analogy is that the formal court system can sometimes feel stuffy and elitist, but it does a much better job of defending the rights of vulnerable individuals than the alternative, mob justice.  At their best, institutions can vest power in ideas rather than people, and thereby decentralize that power.

This is why Anthropic has always made its policy proposals very carefully.  We try very hard to make proposals that disadvantage (slow down) frontier AI companies while *advantaging* smaller competitors.  California’s SB53 (which we supported), and even the much-maligned SB 1047 (which we were ambivalent on), completely exempt any company below a certain amount of revenue or model training costs from being covered at all (it was $500M for SB 53, lower for 1047 but we objected to that).  More recently the testing process we’ve advocated for at CAISI and the White House involves more rigorous tests for frontier models than off-frontier models — something that differentially advantages challengers.  Similarly, the “Pacing the Frontier” letter envisions (or at least Anthropic’s preferred implementation of it envisions) modulating the pace of the very best models while not constraining those who are catching up.  This hurts the business interests of the frontier labs and helps challengers, including open-weights!

Overall my view is that AI is *structurally* a technology that tends to concentrate power, for reasons that have nothing to do with regulation (more to do with the extreme implications of the scaling laws).  Open-weights do help some with this but are nowhere near a sufficient solution because they simply shift the concentration somewhat to those with the most compute and chips (which are roughly the frontier labs plus maybe hardware providers).  By contrast I think the right “rules of the road” can simultaneously (a) address AI’s cyber/bio/alignment risks, (b) institutionally constrain the power of the frontier AI companies, and (c) leave room for open-weights models while also addressing the specific risks that they bring.

BTW I do not think that the events of the last few months have “failed to result in [my] preferred regulatory path”.  The approach that the Trump administration is reported to be taking — pre-deployment testing for frontier models, and also testing of open-weights models when they get closer to the frontier — is one that I am very supportive of, though of course I have to see the details to be sure.  I am also supportive of Demis Hassabis’ ideas around a FINRA-like entity.  This contrasts with six months ago when most of the industry was still pushing for preemption of all state regulation and no apparent federal approach either.

items.title: 2/2 Second, on the messaging around AI.  I do not agree that my messaging has been disproportionately negative.  In fact
items.content:
2/2 Second, on the messaging around AI.  I do not agree that my messaging has been disproportionately negative.  In fact it has been about equally balanced between risks and benefits: I’ve written one major essay about each, and even in interviews where I discuss the risks, I make sure to frequently mention the incredible benefits as well as proposing possible solutions to the risks (short clips from my interviews that end up on social media tend to be disproportionately negative, as that gets clicks).  In fact, I wrote Machines of Loving Grace because I didn’t feel the AI industry was painting an inspiring enough picture of how the technology could radically transform the world for the better.  The bulk of the essay is devoted to refuting skepticism of AI’s potential in health and biology, and showing why I think it will actually be possible to cure most human disease in ~5-10 years, as crazy as it may sound to ordinary people and frankly to biologists as well (I used to be one!).  And, if you read my most recent essay (Policy on the AI Exponential), I discuss concrete proposals for how to streamline the FDA process to make sure the deluge of AI-accelerated drugs isn’t slowed down by the regulatory process.  I feel the urgency here: I lost my father to Hepatitis C only a few years before the development of direct-acting antivirals (sofosbuvir), which cure 95% of patients and probably would have cured him.

I do agree that the public has a negative view of AI (and that this is a big problem), but I don’t think it is primarily caused by me or any other AI leader warning about AI’s risks.  I think it is fundamentally a crisis of trust.  I think that ordinary people don’t trust companies, governments, or the tech industry and always suspect that we are cooking up some new way to screw them over.  The causes of this go back decades and AI is just the latest iteration of it.  I don’t think that a glitzy marketing campaign with a positive spin (which some have advocated that Anthropic do) is the way to win back that trust — at this point, saying that AI will cure cancer is more a cliche than it is inspiring, and most people think it is deceptive.  The thing that will work is *actually curing cancer*.  I think by far the most accurate criticism of AI companies including Anthropic is that we haven’t yet delivered on our big promises to benefit the world.  That is totally on us, and I think it’s the criticism you should be making, instead of all this stuff about messaging and marketing.

We are however doing our best to fix this: Anthropic is ramping up its efforts very quickly in biology and medicine, and we hope to have incredible results in the coming years and some early glimmers in the coming months.  When we’ve actually accomplished something real, the whole world will hear about it, as loudly as possible, you have my word on that.  But until then I don’t want to make empty promises, and in the meantime I feel compelled to speak honestly about the very real risks of AI and how to address them.  Honesty is the right thing on the merits, and in terms of public credibility and trust it is no worse than, and may in fact be better than, an approach that ignores or distracts from risks which people instinctively understand are real.

Send this to ANYONE on your team using AI agents with Claude/Codex skills:

If I were you, I'd put your BEST AI skills in a GitHub repo, turn that repo into a PLUGIN, and have your team INSTALL it in Claude/Codex with auto update on.  

Why?

1. Everyone gets the same AI SOPs instead of 10 versions floating around Slack

2. When one person improves a skill, the whole team gets the better version.

3. New hires can start with your best workflows instead of a blank AI setup (this is a BIG deal).

4. If someone breaks a skill, you can roll it back with version control.

5. Personal skills can stay personal, while team skills become shared company infrastructure (and an asset!).

6. Your best AI processes stay with the company when someone leaves.

7. You can chain skills together for bigger workflows, like titles -> thumbnails -> descriptions -> YouTube publish.

8. You can track which skills are actually being used and delete the ones collecting dust.

9. You get less slop because the agent has real instructions, examples, taste, and process.

10. Your team moves from single-player AI to multiplayer AI.

(thanks to @aiwithremy for coming onto @startupideaspod)

Watch full breakdown here (clearly explained): https://t.co/cvIuFBhOEB 

I don't know why I didn't do this before.

The more I think about it, the more obvious it feels: your AI workflows should be version controlled company assets.

It kinda feels like the difference between “we use AI” and “we actually operate with AI".

Enjoy.

items.content:
NOT enough attention is being given to:

1) Claude dynamic workflows. Claude is literally generating a harness on demand! Agents spinning up 400 agents to run something in parallel and bringing it back to you, when all you did was ask for the outcome in natural language. 

2) Claude Tag. Proactive AI just *feels* different. We don’t have to invoke it, we don’t have to ask it anything, it’s just THERE. And it helps. We’ve brought it in to several slack channels to test it out and are still working through tool connections which are annoying. 

3) Codex live voice mode. Some will say it’s an ambient chief of staff. I think that undersells it. It’s an ambient workforce, an ambient voice-controlled operating system. I go on walks, talk to AI, fire off multiple computer tasks, triage my day, and improve my system architecture…all via natural language and yapping.

items.title:
The best upgrade to Claude Code is a folder structure.

This is why it works: the model is already strong enough. What i
items.content:
The best upgrade to Claude Code is a folder structure.

This is why it works: the model is already strong enough. What it does not have is your context. Put that context in the repo, and the same model ships better work. 

3 markdown files carry most of it:

1) CLAUDE md:
- The operating manual. It tells Claude how you want it to work.
- Small, reviewable changes. A plan before it edits product behavior. Your existing code style.
- Then the business in one line: the buyer, the pain, the promise.

2) Roadmap md:
- It tells Claude what matters this week.
- A landing page, a waitlist form, a demo flow, 10 Looms to med spa owners.
- Then the out of scope list: payments, CRM integration, admin dashboards, multi-user permissions. That list keeps it on the MVP.

3) Review md: 
- It tells Claude how to judge the work before it ships.
- Does the change match the roadmap? Is it small enough to review? Are there mobile layout issues?
- And for a landing page: "can a first-time visitor understand the offer in five seconds?"

Once you have those files, organize the folders around them: 
- /app is the product
- /context is "the business brain."
- /customers holds the sales calls, the objections, the words your customers use.
- /demos holds the Loom scripts.
- /routines holds the recurring prompts.

Then end your setup prompt with one line: "ask me for any missing context that would materially change the setup." The then asks any questions it still has and only then does it begin building

The catch: the structure does not remove the review. 

Opus or Fable 5 do very good work with the right files, but "it does need these guardrails," and without them it will "trip here and there." 

So write the 3 files before you you begin building your first feature.

items.content:
1. Factor ETFs are often not orthogonalized to other factors and are themselves a myriad of factors. Often times due to long-only construction. Whilst one could argue they are more "actionable", they are most definitely not "better" at representing the underlying factors for analysis.

2. "High IQ"/professional/institutional factor models are constructed using the mfm methodology where beta is observed and returns are estimated. 

This is not intuitive for non-quants since returns are normally the observed variables. See https://t.co/BsS2kS5LBR.

That's where the "numbers" come from.

3. Multi factor models (the real stuff) has been used extensively to great success at all real quant firms. One could probably get away with NOT using MFMs, or using a watered down version of them, but it's certainly not a gimmick!

Launch HN: OneCLI (YC S26) – OSS sandboxed agent harness for teams Hi HN, Jonathan & Guy here from OneCLI, an agent harness built for teams, giving every employee a secured, sandboxed personal agent.

Here’s what you can do with it:

1. get a sandboxed agent, with all the OneCLI capabilities in place like connect your GitHub account, Gmail, Notion, or Dropbox simply from the chat.

2. deterministic human in the loop approval in the chat itself for things that you need 100% control like sending an email or deleting the Linear ticket.

3. manage team policy in one place, enforced across every agent in the workspace

4. enjoy global connections at the team level, like shared LLM keys or service accounts

Here’s a demo: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=dlW-44ntpbE

We started working on this by accident, even though our careers were in the security space. We were working on a devtool called ChartDB, an open-source DB tool. When OpenClaw took off back in January, we started using it to orchestrate agents on top of ChartDB. We quickly understood there is a big issue around auth. Agents need credentials to do real work, but to give them those secrets would not be the best idea. They keep them in their memory and also write them down to local files and their sessions as plain text. And we knew that agents can easily be fooled into giving up those API keys/secrets. So we needed some way to control the agent and stop prompt injections from tricking it into using its services for an attacker's benefit.

We created OneCLI that started as a vault for AI Agents built in Rust.

We found out that most of our demand for OneCLI came from autonomous agents like Hermes, OpenClaw and NanoClaw for individuals and teams.

Users looked for useful agents that do things for the person who runs them with two missing parts: 1) managing secrets and permissions. 2) and for teams - multiplayer management.

We decided to pivot and provide the agent itself as a harness for teams, to give each employee an agent. We saw that teams had to deal with setting up their own harness again and again, and basically as we already had the vault as a gateway. We got the idea to provide the missing piece of the agent management out of the box and open source it (Apache-2.0, with a small enterprise exception).

We're open source first - the entire platform, not just a small portion of it like other agents, so companies can actually see the code, evaluate it, and trust it instead of taking our word for it. They run it isolated, in their own environment, fully under their control, at production quality, not a locked black box hosted somewhere else. That means the safety isn't just a promise, it's something they can verify themselves. Combined with real autonomy and least-privilege access, that's what makes it something a company can fully own and trust, not just adopt.

We also approach this from a company perspective rather than an individual one. Our solution manages agents on behalf of each employee, wrapped in deterministic guardrails that company admins configure through centralized policies.

For the agent engine itself we’re using jcode which is the core of the agent-loop. We found out that it improves the experience and makes the agent smarter and faster.

Here’s how it works:

It runs on infra you control. Fully open-source, self-host or cloud in minutes.

The agent never holds a real secret. It gets a placeholder. The real credential is injected at the gateway, per request, after the call is authorized. It never enters the agent's context, memory, or logs.

Enforcement outside the model. Prompts are suggestions. Policies defined by the org admin run at the network layer, outside the agent and the LLM. Block endpoints, rate limit per agent, require approval, scope per employee. The gateway decides. The agent can't bypass it.

Isolated VM per agent. Own memory, own keys, own permissions. Blast radius is one agent.

Speed of the Harness: Rust engine under the agent loop.

Full identity trail. Every agent is bound to an employee. Every call logged with who it acted for and which policy allowed it.

Some things people are doing with the platform include:

- Managing their company life cycle entirely from the sales calls, to the product side automatically open tickets to the engineering teams, that would kick the development agents to deliver and ship to production.

- Operational side, like automatically hygiene the CRM after calls, sourcing leads, book meetings and manage follow ups emails.

- Some of our customers also doing their entire grocery shopping using those agents and send them to take care of their chores like ordering things online.

About the team: Both founders come from cybersecurity backgrounds. Jonathan spent years at Axis Security building zero trust network access. The core idea is that you never trust the client. You decide exactly what a person can reach, and you enforce it outside of them, at the network layer, so it doesn't matter what the client tries to do. That's how every serious company gives access to humans today. Guy was the 1st employee in Argon security doing AppSec.

We would love to hear your thoughts on the move, happy to get issues open to improve and get your agent to be powerful and secure - designed for teams, not just individuals.

items.content:
One of my favorite ways to use Claude Code is to create a ticket

Here is why I love it: Claude Code is very good at doing the work, but it must know when it's "done." A ticket gives Claude Code a clear signpost for when to stop

Here's how to write it in 4 parts:

1) Give it a job:
- "Add a wait list form to the landing page."

2)  Give it a proper scope:
- Ask for a name, an email, and a company.

3) Tell it the UX you want:
- Show a simple success message after a person sends the form.

4) Tell the constraints it needs to follow:
- Keep the design the same as the current brand identity.

Then add an instruction: make the change small enough to review in the diff view, run the checks, open the app in the desktop preview, and tell me what still needs human review.

The catch: a ticket that is not clear makes Claude guess. "Make the app better." "Add AI." "Build the whole thing." You get a diff too big to read, so you cannot tell if it is right.

Keep the ticket small enough so that Claude knows exactly what to do

items.content:
If you want to build your first AI employee the easiest thing to do is create a morning brief agent.

Here's why it works: the task is "useful and controlled." It goes through your business overnight and leaves a to do list

Set it up in 3 parts:

1) The morning brief.
- Every weekday at 7am it reads /customers, /context, and your open GitHub issues.
- It writes /context/morning-brief.md.
- Top customer pain point. One product risk. One build task for today. One question to ask a customer. 
- Under 500 words. No production code. No pull request.

2) The weekly ops review.
- Every Friday at 3pm it reads the open issues and the recent customer notes.
- It groups the related issues and finds the duplicates.
- One fix for the week, written to /context/weekly-ops.md.

3) The pull request loop.
- When a pull request opens, it reviews the code against review.md.
- It comments only on bugs, broken user flows, security problems, and confusing behavior.
- Then it tells you if the work is ready for a human.

Two routines and one loop. Each one takes a few seconds to set up.

The catch: It's boring but this is what people mean by the "night shift," it reads and catalogs business operations into markdowns so that you don't have to spend your time doing this busy work. 

So find similar tasks your team spends hours every week doing and give them to Claude to handle.

items.content:
Skills are just SOPs for AI.

An SOP is the document you give a new employee so the job gets done your way on the first day. 

Claude is a new employee in every new chat. 

So here's how I create my skills: 

1) The trigger:
- The one line that starts the job.
- "create a proposal for x to sponsor the newsletter."

2) The steps: 
- The process in the order you do it.

3) The preferences:
- The colors. The logo.
- The price at the bottom, not the top.

4) The file:
- One markdown file.
- Claude reads it when you need the job done

5) The correction: 
- Run it again in a new chat.
-  Read the result.
- Correct the file, not the chat.

Before I built my skills, every time I needed the same doc I had to walk Claude through my style all over again.

Yesterday I typed the trigger line and it one-shot the proposal.

The catch: the skill has to be tight. A loose document gives you a loose result, and most people blame the model for that.

So find the one job you do the same way every time. Write a dialed skill

items.content:
The best way to make an AI agent faster is a permission list.

Here is why it works: you delegate to an agent the same way you do to an employee: safe tasks, permissioned tasks, blocked tasks. Sort each task into one of the three groups, and you always know how much room the agent has. 

A clear breakdown of each bucket:

1) Safe actions:
- Read files and inspect the code base.
- Propose plans and run local tests.
- Edit a small feature branch, update the docs, open a draft pull request.

2) Ask-first actions:
- Install dependencies.
- Change a database migration or touch authentication.
- Change the payment logic.
- Delete files.

3) Human-owned actions: 
- Production deploys.
- Customer data decisions.
- Billing decisions.
- Security-sensitive changes.

Then set the permission mode in Claude Desktop to match. Start with strict limits. 

Use plan mode for the large changes. Use manual review while you learn the system. 

Give the agent more access as your repo notes, your review checklist, and your task scopes get stronger. 

So start your permission list today and sort each task accordingly

items.content:
I gave Claude Code "eyes" so it can check its work

Here is why you should do it: a build is not a check. A good employee does the task and then checks the task. They open the product, click the flow, run tests, look for errors.

Here's how to do it in 5 steps:

1) Getting Started:
- Tell it to run the app, not only to write the code.
- Open the landing page in the desktop preview.

2) Assign it a role:
- Give it a persona. Mine was a med spa owner who sees the page for the first time.
- Then tell it to check the implementation based on the user behavior of your ICP

3) Give it questions that it should investigate:
- What does the buyer understand in the first 5 seconds?
- What feels "confusing or low trust"?
- Does the form work, and what happens after submission?

4) Tell it to document the results:
- It clicked "join the waitlist" with an empty form.
- It used four tools. It read the page. It used a computer.
- It checked the record in the backend, then the console and the network for errors.

5) Limit it to 1 pass:
- Ask for a single focus pass on "the highest impact issue".
- Mine: the page asks a cold owner for an email, with no word about spam.
- The fix was "expectation setting microcopy at the CTA".

Why this is so powerful: A page can load and still be confusing. A form can submit and still feel awkward. A button can be on the page and still be hard to see.

So have Claude review its work every time. The eyes are underrated.

items.content:
How to prompt Claude Fable-5 (and any AI model):

→ Start by deleting the long examples you give.
→ Delete the "step-by-step" prompt technique. 
→ Avoid biased questions. Don't finish with "right?"
→ Chain-of-Thought (step-by-step) only works well with maths problems. It's worth skipping it.
→ Don't give a long list of rules (max 3) to follow. 

The models got very good at simple prompts, and worse at your complicated, over-structured ones.

To make a simple prompt, better:

→ Make your next prompt shorter.
→ Define the goals with extreme clarity.
→ Give no more than 3 rules to perform one task.
→ Ask open-ended questions to let it figure it out.
→ Always encourage it to ask clarifying questions.
→ Don't trust the sources blindly. It tries to prove itself by finding links that agree with what it already has written.

This is the one simple prompt template I stick to:

"[GOAL: What a finished answer must achieve. Write the test it has to pass.]
[CONTEXT: The facts the AI would otherwise invent. Only the ones it cannot know.]
[CONSTRAINTS: The hard limits. 3 max.]
If anything here is missing or unclear, ask me before you answer.
[Add “use AskUserQuestion tool” if you’re on Claude]."

I've been teaching prompt engineering since 2022, and so much has changed since then.

What was true - because science said so - isn't anymore. The models are 10x more capable now.

I'm a psycho so I actually filter out and read the 100+ daily papers on prompt engineering (on arxiv. org). Read my findings at https://t.co/BhdLRaCgvy.

One of the best uses of Claude Code's plan mode is the brief you write before you start it.

Here is why it works: You talk it through what you are planning to do. Claude reads the project, thinks about the job, and shows you the approach before it changes a file. 

Write the brief in 5 parts:

1) Context:
- Tell it to inspect the current app first.
- CLAUDE.md, roadmap.md, review.md.
- This is the step people skip. Do not skip it.

2) Scope:
- The files it must change.
- The smallest clean implementation.

3) Experience
- What the user sees. The one-line promise.

4) Risk:
- What can go wrong. Spam and abuse.
- How you will verify the work.

5) The cut.
- What it purposely leaves out of v1

Then add one more line: "wait for my approval before editing." 

Now you have something to build off of before starting.

The catch: the first plan is not perfect. It doesn't need to be. You iterate until you feel good about starting the coding process

It sounds like this: Keep the front end only. Connect it to Supabase, because you want real submissions. Cut the form to name, email, company. "Don't touch auth and payments or the database yet."

So take the next real piece of work in your project. Write the brief, not the prompt. "Measure twice, cut once."

items.content:
When Claude writes the code in minutes, the review becomes the work.

Here is why: the build is fast so all the work has shifted to checking the work. Did it solve the correct problem? Did it change the correct files? 

Here's my 4 layer review process: 

1) Your read:
- Open the diff view in Claude Desktop.
- Look at each file that Claude touched.
- Ask three questions: does this match the ticket, does this match the plan, is there something surprising here?
- Surprising changes show you the risk. If Claude must add a waitlist form, and it also changes authentication, routing and the database, stop and look.

2) Your standard:
- Write a review.md file before the work starts.
- Then tell Claude: "use review as the standard".

3) The sort:
- Ask for production issues, broken edge cases and confusing user flows.
- Ask for files changed outside the scope of the ticket.
- Ask Claude to put each item into must fix, should fix, or okay to ship.

4) The deep check:
- /review for usual changes.
- /ultra review for authentication, payments, and other risky work. It starts a remote session for the full repository.

The catch: layer 2 only works if you wrote the review.md first. Claude cannot compare the work to a standard that does not exist.

Since I've implemented this process, I have caught dozens of bugs that would've made it to production.

items.content:
This Unitree robot is nine feet tall, weighs half a ton, and has a cockpit in its chest that a human can climb into.

The GD01 walks on two legs or four, and costs $650,000.

When TIME visited Unitree’s Hangzhou headquarters, their founder Wang Xingxing wouldn’t get in or even turn it on, because “It might not be safe,” he said.

That’s a striking thing to hear from the biggest humanoid maker in the world, a company shipping over 5,500 units last year.

It just filed for a $6B IPO, and has pushed its flagship G1 down to $13,500 by building its own actuators, the motors that make up most of a humanoid’s cost.

But the numbers underneath tell a stranger story. Only 9% of its humanoid sales go to real industrial work.

74% go to universities and developers, meaning the industry is largely selling robots to people trying to build better robots.

Hardware is racing ahead. The software that makes these machines genuinely useful is still the hard part.

items.content:
I don’t really have a process for figuring out what the future is going to look like. It’s the one thing I’ve always just kind of been able to do pretty well, and haven’t really been able to teach anyone. A lot of it really is just gut feeling, combined with some high-level data.

One mistake I see people making is getting too deep into the weeds, they usually find a million things that will break the overall thesis. Everything has roadblocks, you’re mostly looking at the incentives to build towards the future and break those, and the high-level physics of the thing (i’m not even close to an expert on this so I just read a lot and try to form my own opinions, + gut)

I do have a very small fund, but I don’t really have an interest right now in running a much larger one. I think part of why I’m good at this is that it’s not a full-time job for me. I don’t screen companies. When I find something I want to invest in, I reach out. That’s pretty much it. If I were screening companies all day, I would probably be doing much worse.

Plus, I just really like building and sharing what I learn. A big part of my personal goal right now is just to help as many people as possible understand what’s coming down the pipe with AI. Feels like our moral imperative at this point and very few people are doing it in a way that’s understandable to the average person.

I could probably make more money investing, raise a huge fund, fees, carry, etc., but I think right now, the world needs a clear understanding of what is happening, much more than I need some carry lol. And no one seems to be doing that well (SV folks love to talk in jargon).

That said, if anyone wants to convince me to start a big fund, happy to chat about it. But I don’t like your odds. :)

Sorry if this is confusingly worded, it’s late and I’ve had a very long day

items.content:
About half the time I have a thesis that I’m really convinced of (to the level of that, if I had the time, I would go and start that type of company myself)… then I go out and try to find the best team in the space.

The other ~half of the time, I just see something and I’m like “holy fuck”, dig in, and if I’m excited enough, I contact the founder.

People overthink this shit. Just figure out what the world is gonna look like a few years out, what’s going to be needed, if there’s actually business value under the tech or if it’ll be commoditized etc., if there’s a real compounding edge, and then invest in the company that’s most likely to win.

A big mistake I see people make is investing in a non-top-tier company in a category because the valuation is better, they get more ownership, etc. I’d rather just pick the likely winner at 3x the price.

items.content:
If you’ve been anywhere near @CantonNetwork Twitter lately, you’ve probably noticed @Oneswapcc keeps showing up in other people’s announcements. 

Not as a sponsor, not as a guest, but as infrastructure, quietly embedded inside apps that have nothing to do with being a DEX. 

A media site, a payments app, a credit protocol. Different products, same swap engine underneath.

@Oneswapcc is a permissionless, non-custodial DEX built natively on Canton, widely seen as the most accessible way for everyday users to swap Canton-native assets like CC and USDCx without going through an institution or centralized exchange. 

No KYC, and funds stay in the user’s wallet until a swap actually settles. 

Since the v2 upgrade shipped in July, swaps also settle atomically, in a single transaction, in line with Canton’s CIP-56 standard. That release shipped an upgraded SDK too, and that’s the piece that’s made the last few weeks possible.

The shift is in how projects are integrating. 

Earlier on, a project would list a token on @Oneswapcc and call it a partnership. 

Now apps are pulling OneSwap’s swap functionality directly inside their own product, so users never have to leave. 

That started back in June with Edel Finance, HandlPay, and Loop Wallet embedding the SDK. 

Last week alone, Alpend, a Canton credit protocol, brought OneSwap on as an execution venue for liquidations, giving collateral a direct on-chain exit path. 

Around the same time, CanPayAI integrated the SDK for in-app swaps, with AI-agent support said to be coming next, and OneSwap marked over five platforms now running its SDK. 

Then just earlier this week, CantonNews went live with OneSwap embedded straight into its website, readers can swap CC, USDCx, EDELx, CBTCx, HANDL, and HECTO without leaving the page.

That’s a handful of embeds inside a couple weeks, not a slow trickle of partnerships.

Every one of these is a small bet that compounds. 

When a project embeds OneSwap instead of building its own swap engine, it’s routing its liquidity and user activity through OneSwap’s infrastructure by default. Enough of that, and OneSwap isn’t one DEX among several on Canton, it’s the settlement layer underneath most of them. 

That’s a harder thing to compete with than just getting users to show up on your own site, and OneSwap’s SDK terms give integrators a cut of the fees their integration generates, so builders have a direct incentive to plug in rather than build around it.

It also tracks with where Canton is pointed. The network is built for institutional-grade infrastructure with privacy and compliance baked in via CIP-56, and a DEX that settles atomically and plugs cleanly into that standard is exactly the kind of DeFi Canton needs sitting on top of its institutional rails.
OneSwap was also flagged in Palladium Labs’ “State of Canton H1 2026” report for its dual role as DEX and embeddable SDK layer, part of a broader maturing of Canton’s production layer this year. 

The July upgrade wasn’t just a version bump, it was the technical unlock that made this pace of shipping possible.

At this pace, OneSwap isn’t trying to win attention one launch at a time. It’s just becoming the thing quietly running underneath everything else on Canton.

Multiple players will emerge with great packaged "agent in a box" solutions. 

The ingredients are simple. A sandbox with an agent inside. 

Alpha is in 

- fast sleep/resume of the sandbox (in a world of node module and rust targets, sandboxes easily become multi GB in size) 
- fast productive harness (pi-like, better if native) 
- well designed auth delegation (not inherit every human token, but also not too constrained to stop it every step) 
- tighter integration with the code and with production. (This is easier said than done - just giving github & sentry MCPs is not enough) 

Getting the whole package right is a massive compute-infra engineering challenge at scale. I feel so fortunate to see this from the inside taking shape. 

All big companies like Google, Meta, Uber, Microsoft have been making their own versions as well. 

Mid sized companies will end up building this on top of Cloudflare Agents SDK and Vercel Sandboxes.
